q: Write isBalanced(text) that returns true when every (), [] and {} in the text is closed in the correct order.
a: Scan once with a stack of open brackets; on a closer, the top must be its matching opener; the stack must be empty at the end.
explanation: Each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening bracket, which is exactly last-in-first-out, so a stack gives an O(n) single pass. Map closers to openers so the check is one lookup. Return false immediately on a closer with an empty stack, and remember that leftover openers also mean the text is unbalanced.
mistake: Counting brackets of each type instead of tracking order, which accepts "([)]".
rubric: Uses a stack and explains why order matters
Handles a closer with an empty stack
Rejects leftover openers at the end
States O(n) time and O(n) space
followups: How would you report the position of the first error?
How would you ignore brackets inside string literals?

q: Write topWords(text, top) that returns the most frequent lowercase words with their counts, highest first, ties alphabetical.
a: Extract words with a regex, count with groupingBy().eachCount(), sort by count descending then word, and take(top).
explanation: This tests fluent use of the collections API and precise ordering. groupingBy { }.eachCount() counts without a manual map. A comparator built with compareByDescending { count }.thenBy { word } makes ties deterministic, which matters for tests and for users. Validate a negative limit instead of letting take() throw an unclear error.
mistake: Sorting only by count, which makes the order of tied words unpredictable.
rubric: Extracts words with a clear definition of a word
Counts with groupingBy/eachCount or an equivalent map
Sorts by count then alphabetically
Validates the limit argument
followups: How would you handle a 10 GB input file?
When would you prefer a Sequence over a List here?

q: Fix the LruCache class so it evicts the least recently used entry and treats get() as a use.
a: Use LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true and override removeEldestEntry to return size > capacity.
explanation: The buggy version keeps insertion order, so get() never refreshes recency, and it evicts entries.keys.last(), the newest entry, instead of the oldest. It also evicts when overwriting an existing key. LinkedHashMap(initialCapacity, loadFactor, accessOrder = true) moves an entry to the end on every read or write, and removeEldestEntry evicts the head only when the map actually grows beyond capacity.
mistake: Evicting before checking whether the key already exists, which drops an entry on an update.
rubric: Identifies that get() does not refresh recency
Identifies that the newest entry is evicted
Uses access order and removeEldestEntry correctly
Mentions thread safety as a separate concern
followups: How would you make this cache thread-safe?
How would you add time-based expiry?

q: Write retry(times, initialDelayMs, maxDelayMs, sleep, block) with capped exponential backoff and an injectable sleep function.
a: Loop attempts 1 until times, returning on success and sleeping with a doubling capped delay on failure; run the final attempt outside the try so its exception propagates.
explanation: Injecting sleep keeps the function deterministic and testable, the same reason production code injects a clock or dispatcher. Doubling the delay with a cap prevents retry storms. Do not sleep after the last attempt, and rethrow the final error rather than wrapping or swallowing it. In coroutine code, use delay and never catch CancellationException, or cancellation stops working.
mistake: Sleeping after the final failed attempt, or swallowing the last exception and returning null.
rubric: Validates arguments
Doubles the delay with a cap
Does not sleep after the final attempt
Propagates the final exception
Explains testability from the injected sleep
followups: How would you add jitter, and why?
How would this change as a suspend function that must stay cancellable?
Which errors should never be retried?

q: Implement a TokenBucket rate limiter with a capacity, a refill rate per second, and an injected clock.
a: Store fractional tokens and the last update time; on each call refill by elapsed time times rate, cap at capacity, then take one token if at least one is available.
explanation: Token buckets allow short bursts up to capacity while enforcing an average rate. Refill lazily on each call instead of using a timer thread. Keep fractional tokens so slow rates work, cap at capacity so idle time cannot build an unlimited burst, and guard against a clock moving backwards. Injecting the clock makes the behaviour testable without sleeping. Shared limiters need synchronization or an atomic compare-and-set.
mistake: Refilling without capping at capacity, or using a background timer instead of computing tokens from elapsed time.
rubric: Refills lazily from elapsed time
Caps tokens at capacity
Handles fractional refill rates
Handles a clock moving backwards
Addresses thread safety
followups: How would you share one limit across several servers?
How does a token bucket differ from a fixed window counter?
